articles.title: Before Robert Downey Jr., These 3 Marvel Stars Who Were Never on Set as Their Beloved Characters Either
articles.summary: Just because you're involved in the Marvel Cinematic Universe doesn't mean you’ll be spending months on a film set as a superhero in costume. The franchise has also seen some of its most unique characters brought to life by actors who never actually had to appear on camera as those characters. It's one of the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Just because you're involved in the Marvel Cinematic Universe doesn't mean you’ll be spending months on a film set as a superhero in costume. The franchise has also seen some of its most unique characters brought to life by actors who never actually had to appear on camera as those characters. It's one of the more peculiar parts of contemporary filmmaking, especially as these are characters that have become so iconic to the MCU. And while Robert Downey Jr. may be the biggest face of Marvel, he's not the only star who was involved in Marvel movies in a way you wouldn't expect.

From talking trees to profanity-loving raccoons, Marvel has used a few big names to sprinkle some personality onto its digital characters. But the actors who voice those characters aren't always the people who make them look real on set. Here are three that may catch you off guard.

Howard the Duck may not be the most obvious Marvel character you'd think of as a major player, but he is one of the more entertaining recurring surprises in the MCU . The wisecracking alien, voiced by Seth Green, initially appeared in the post-credits scene of Guardians of the Galaxy , returning in a few other Marvel films since. Green's role is notable because Howard is brought to life through computer-generated imagery, with Green providing the character's voice rather than physically portraying the duck.

Green has been a regular presence in film and TV for decades (a brief sample includes Austin Powers , The Office , and Robot Chicken ), but his performance as Howard is a more unusual one. You don't have to put on an elaborate costume, spend ages in makeup, or have someone else pretend to be an anthropomorphic duck—Green is the personality that makes Howard's segments work, especially with his sarcastic humor. He reprised his role for Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 . There isn't the same evidence confirming that Green has never appeared on a Marvel set, but this is another clear example of an actor closely associated with a character that he's never physically portrayed, despite spending a lot of time working on the role.

Even though he may be one of Hollywood's most popular actors, Cooper's role in the MCU is somewhat unorthodox. He's the voice behind one of the most lovable (yet irritating) characters in the MCU, the foul-mouthed and emotionally fragile Rocket Raccoon in the Guardians of the Galaxy movies . But Cooper himself has never stepped onto a Guardians set before. In fact, someone else plays the animated Rocket, and you may be surprised.

James Gunn's brother, Sean Gunn, was on set to perform Rocket's movements and expressions, giving the animators a physical reference for bringing the character to life. It's an interesting set-up, especially given how much of Rocket's personality comes through in his facial expressions and how he moves. Bradley Cooper and Sean Gunn worked really well together in bringing Rocket to life, for sure. James Gunn clarified the set-up when addressing a fan, revealing that neither Cooper nor Vin Diesel had ever set foot on a Guardians of the Galaxy set, which is incredible when you think about it.

The strangest of the strange casting choices in the MCU is surely Vin Diesel's take on the character of Groot. The star of the Fast & Furious movies has lent his voice to a character that is probably one of the most popular Marvel characters out there: a walking, talking tree who is known for uttering just three words. Nonetheless, even Groot—who isn't one to speak much in the franchise as of yet—is provided with a voice thanks to Diesel.

Similar to Bradley Cooper, Diesel has never set foot on a Guardians of the Galaxy set in order to embody his character. Instead, other actors create both the look and the movements of Groot,with Krystian Godlewski serving as Groot's physical reference performer in the original movie, followed by Terry Notary in Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame. Austin Freeman also performed Groot on set for Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3. Diesel, meanwhile, supplies the voice and records various ways he could have said the character's series of one-word lines, so audiences can understand what Groot is actually saying. As James Gunn explained in an interview, Diesel even gets special scripts that reveal the meaning behind each of the character's words. It's a unique take on voice acting, and one that makes so much sense for a character who's arguably become the most emotional component of the franchise. And who knew that "I am Groot" could have so many different meanings?

articles.title: A Cult '80s Character Had His Final TV Appearance 36 Years Ago, And He Wasn't Officially Back for Decades
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Netflix The '80s were a pretty amazing time in pop culture, speaking as someone who is from there. While the '50s and '60s got decades of glaze from the silent generation and the baby boomers and '70s nostalgia faded away as quickly as any fond memories of that decade, the '80s have stayed pop culturally relevant […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The '80s were a pretty amazing time in pop culture, speaking as someone who is from there. While the '50s and '60s got decades of glaze from the silent generation and the baby boomers and '70s nostalgia faded away as quickly as any fond memories of that decade, the '80s have stayed pop culturally relevant for much longer than most decades. It was the beginning of an era of commercialization the likes of which we'd never seen before. '80s pop culture is another level from previous decades. Even the youngest zoomers can name more '80s pop cultural references than any other decade. I don't know what kind of toys my parents and their friends played with, but every one in the English-speaking world knows the ones I did. Into this pop cultural landscape walked Pee-Wee Herman and 36 years ago, he made one of his last official appearance.

Pee-Wee Herman was played by the late great comedian Paul Reubens. He had debuted the character on the Hollywood comedy club circuit in the late '70s, creating the character in 1977 while a member of the Groundlings, the legendary LA improv group. Pee-Wee After an HBO special, Herman would break into pop culture in 1985 in Tim Burton's first film , Pee-Wee's Big Adventure . Audiences, whether they be adults or children, fell in love with the character and he would soon find a home on Saturday morning TV with Pee-Wee's Playhouse . He became an icon, but some legal woes led to the end of the character everywhere but in our hearts for years to come.

Paul Reubens' death in 2023 was the end of one of the greatest children's entertainers of all-time. Pee-Wee was first created to be a fun character to play in improv scenes, his childlike wonder and risque double entendres letting him play perfectly off of greats like the late Phil Hartman (one of the finest improv actors ever, bar none). In fact, Reubens and Hartman developed the character together, which if you know the history of Phil Hartman and his talent perfectly explains why the character has worked so well.

Pee-Wee's Big Adventure was the perfect introduction for the character to the rest of the world. Pee-Wee's quest for his red bike was like something out of myth, if myths were written by goth boomers and closeted gay improv actors. Reuben had spent eight years playing the character by the time the movie premiered, so new fans got to see what amounts to the ultimate version of the character. Herman was the kind of kid's character that was both extremely wholesome and also just the right amount of risque, allowing him to appeal to children, older kids, and adults.

Pee-Wee's Playhouse launched a year after the movie and it was amazing. I was an '80s kid, born in 1980, and I watched the show religiously. Saturday mornings were a holy day for children back then, a time of sugary cereals and savory snacks, hours of TV that was made specifically for us, which was quite rare back then. Pee-Wee ' s Playhouse was on CBS, part of one of the best line-ups on network TV, with '80s kids classics like The Berenstain Bears, Jim Henson's Muppet Babies, and Hulk Hogan's Rock and Wrestling (I would mostly watch CBS and ABC, then move to NBC for some Saved By the Bell ; late '80s Saturdays rocked). However, it was actually more like an older kids show, one that has gone down in legend – Mr. Roger's Neighborhood .

Both shows took viewers into the realm of imagination, showing them all of the things that their brains were capable of. There were outlandish characters, both human and puppet, and the perfect setting for each show. But, most importantly, Rogers and Herman both deeply cared about developing children and making sure they grew up right. Both shows had the same kinds of good lessons for kids, ones that helped children become both more independent and more caring about others and the world around them.

One of the things you have to realize about '80s children pop culture is that it was the end of children's entertainment as a learning resource in a lot of ways. The Reagan Administration, always in the pockets of every business willing to pay them, lifted FDA regulations that made sure that children's programming would also be good for children's development and not, say, 30-minute long toy commercials that were often as deep as a puddle (are you starting to understand why the world is like this?). Pee-Wee's Playhouse was made by people who cared about children more than profit and that's part of what made it so great.

From 1986 to 1990 , Pee-Wee's Playhouse put out brilliant new episodes, but like all things on TV, the show would eventually come to an end. In 1990, the ratings had slid enough for the character's show to get cancelled, with the final episode "Playhouse for Sale" airing on November 16th, 1991. The episode was recorded at some point in 1990 (I tried to find out when, but it's not on the Internet anywhere) but wouldn't air until the next year. However, by the time it did air, everything had changed for Reubens.

In July of 1991, Reubens was arrested for indecent exposure at a pornography theater (yes, there was a time when watching porn was a communal activity). His mugshot looked nothing like the clean cut Pee-Wee we were used to and the whole thing shocked everyone. Many assumed that the show was ended because of the arrest, but this wasn't the case at all. However, the incident was the nail in the coffin for Pee-Wee Herman. The character was all but dead, with Reubens moving on and taking other roles. It was the last time the character would appear on network TV in his own show.

Paul Reubens' 1991 arrest hurt the legacy of Pee-Wee Herman at first, but in the years since, most people have realized that the whole situation was nowhere near as bad as it was portrayed as. Pee-Wee's Playhouse is judged not by the one time the cops decided to mess with (gay) men at a movie theater where they weren't hurting anyone, but for how great of a kids' show it was. It grabbed the baton passed by Mr. Rogers and Jim Henson and the Muppet Factory and ran with it, creating a children's show that has becme a legend.

The end of Pee-Wee's Playhouse wasn't the last time we'd see the character, though. Reubens would appear as Pee-Wee at numerous shows, even appearing in a well-loved SNL sketch with Andy Samberg. Pee-Wee's Playhouse would air in syndication on Fox and Cartoon Network in the late '90s and '00s, introducing all-new fans to the show, but it wouldn't be until 2016 that the character would return in his own production, the Netflix movie Pee-Wee's Big Holiday . It was the last appearance of the character, and a perfect send-off for this beloved icon.

Did you grow up watching Pee-Wee's Playhouse ? What's your favorite Paul Reuben role and why is it Blow ? Sound off in the comment section below.

Spanish actor Karla Sofia Gascon , whose turn in "Emilia Pérez" made her the first transgender actor to land an Oscar nomination, says the controversy that consumed her awards campaign was driven by people who did not want to see someone like her win.

Her Oscar run was overshadowed by a row over old social media posts . "It has never yet been shown that I wrote anything against anyone, nor has it been proven anywhere," she says. "It was just a pile of assumptions, with everyone saying something different, and they created a figure of me that isn't me."

Gascon describes a long awards push as an ordeal for actors, with political interests at play on every side, and says she would rather do her work and let audiences decide whether they like it. Such campaigns, she argues, open the door to people using actors for political or economic ends. "And I think we are here for the art," she says.

Cinema, in her view, carries a social responsibility to show audiences the best of humanity, even as it remains both entertainment and business. Mixing the political, the economic and the talent, she says, dilutes the essence of acting, which for her means bringing lives to other people and making them think.

Transgender people face more and more problems, Gascón says. "We are living through a moment of regression in the rights of transgender people, of sexual diversity." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Global politics, Gascon adds, is making life harder still for people who already face steep odds, and above all for trans people, "who are considered in practically the whole world as the lowest in society." That, she says, is why a campaign arose against "a woman who could win a great award" – a reading she stresses is "not a justification" but "an explanation."

" Emilia Perez ," directed by Jacques Audiard , won Gascon best actress at the Cannes Film Festival, the European Film Awards and the Lumiere Awards, alongside Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations. The biggest change to her career since, she says, is that she no longer has to audition. "I started at 16, I've had a career of more than 30 years and I've done everything in acting," she says.

She has since made the Italian film "Scuola di Seduzione" and "Trinidad." On working across languages and cultures, she says: "It makes me grow as a person, it makes me grow in my work, it makes me understand human beings much more."

Next up is "Las Malas," Armando Bo's adaptation of Camila Sosa Villada's novel, in which she plays Tia Encarna and which she rates among the best work of her life. The film shot for around four months this year in Argentina and Uruguay. Gascon sees many parallels with "Emilia Perez" in the role but would rather discuss it once audiences have seen it, possibly at Cannes or Venice.

During a masterclass at the festival, where she was honored by Chanchal Kumar, secretary of India's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Gascon detailed her "Trinidad" character: a gun-wielding outlaw who uses a wheelchair and serves as the villain of the 19th-century tale. She had hoped for horses and guns when the Western came calling, only to learn she would be playing a woman "in a chair without any movement."

"And when you confront this, you say, 'That's the best opportunity for me to understand other people in this world,'" she told the audience.

Gascon builds every role from the voice outward, seeking a "really soft, really calm" register for the "Trinidad" role. On "Emilia Pérez," she recorded a range of voices on cassette before settling on a deep voice for Manitas and a "delicate" one for Emilia, and came to appreciate the process when dubbing herself later.

She called Audiard the best director she has worked with. "He brings you the liberty to act," Gascón said. "He plays a lot, he laughs a lot, he's really funny, and I think he is a really good friend." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

On set, she said, actors should remember they are one part of a team that can run to hundreds. "I don't want to create conflict on set. I don't want to create a difference between me and the others. I don't want blue flowers in my caravan," she said.

Gascon traced her affection for India to a Madrid screening of Deepa Mehta's "Water" decades ago, and named Indian Oscar winner A.R. Rahman her favorite musician. She also drew parallels between the heightened performance styles of Mexican telenovelas, where she spent much of her career, and Indian cinema, arguing that histrionics and truth are compatible.

She also said filmmakers too often cast to labels such as "Spanish" or "she is a woman" instead of trusting actors' range. "It's nice when Indian people work in Spain, work in the United States. I love when a Russian works in Africa," Gascon said. "I think we are all the same humanity."

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Tom Cruise wasn't the first person book readers thought of when they saw Jack Reacher , but he somehow managed to pull off the role despite being nothing like the character. In 2012, Cruise and his Mission: Impossible director Christopher McQuarrie adapted the Lee Child novel One Shot into a movie and brought Jack Reacher to the big screen. This caused a huge uproar among fans of the novel series since Reacher stands well over six feet tall and is a mass of solid muscle. Cruise is the opposite of that in every way. Despite this, the movie earned positive reviews and good box office, and it warranted a sequel.

Four years later, Cruise returned for the sequel Jack Reacher: Never Go Back and once again proved that he was right for the role, even if he wasn't anything like the character Child created in his book series. Now, 10 years later, Jack Reacher fans have something for all fans.

Jack Reacher: Never Go Back was released on October 21, 2016, and was based on the 2013 Jack Reacher novel Never Go Back . While Cruise and McQuarrie teamed up for the first movie in the series, the follow-up was directed by Edward Zwick, although McQuarrie remained on board as a producer. This film takes place four years after the first movie, and it follows Reacher as he goes on the run with an Army major who was framed for espionage. While on the run, Reacher realizes there is a dark conspiracy at work and finds himself forced to uncover the truth, even as a fugitive.

Cobie Smulders (Maria Hill from the MCU) stars as Major Susan Turner, the woman framed for espionage. While Cruise was someone who never fit the role of Jack Reacher for fans of the books, he was able to pull off the same attitude and nonstop action hero that the book's character introduced. Lee Child fans hated the casting, but movie fans bought into it instantly. The first movie made $218.3 million on a $60 million budget, with a 67% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. The sequel made $162 million on a $60 million budget, and while it dropped in audience and critical scores, it still showed that Cruise could play the action star, even when miscast in the role.

The good news for fans is there are two different versions of Jack Reacher that anyone can enjoy. The fans of the Tom Cruise movies have that version of the character, and the fans of the novel have a physically accurate version on the Prime Video series Reacher , starring Alan Ritchson. In the books, Jack Reacher is six feet five and weighs between 210 and 250 pounds. Tom Cruise is five foot seven and around 160 pounds, nearly a foot shorter and between 50 and 90 pounds lighter. If anything, this made his ability to stand up against overwhelming odds even more impressive.

However, Alan Ritchson is six foot three and built his weight to around 235 to 240 pounds for Reacher, making him the weight of Jack Reacher while standing only two inches shorter. Even though he isn't as tall, he dwarfs most of the people in the show's cast and portrays the monster of a man that Reacher is in the novels. The TV series has run for four seasons, with two more on the way. The average score for the four seasons on Rotten Tomatoes is an impressive 95%, with a 77% audience rating. The second and third seasons have an almost perfect 98% critics score, while the first season has the best audience rating at 91%.

Later-season audience scores dropped into the 70s on Rotten Tomatoes, with the fourth dropping to 64%, which is below that of Tom Cruise's first movie. That shows that the television and movie audiences don't have the same desire to have Reacher novel-accurate as long as the story plays out how they want it to. The novel's fans often reveled in the Jack Reacher fight scenes, and by the fourth season of the show, many audience reviews on Rotten Tomatoes complained about those same moments. While Ritchson's hulking man dispensing justice is what Lee Child fans came to see , the more creative fighting style of someone like Tom Cruise seems to have worked just as well when it comes to audiences.

What are your thoughts on Tom Cruise's portrayal of Jack Reacher? Let us know which version of Reacher you liked better in the comments below.
